verdict.rationale: The lexicon (the inventory of word meanings) establishes the indwelling half of the proposition cleanly and adds a sharp incompatibility word in 2 Corinthians 6:14 to 16, where 'temple of God' (naos theou) is set against 'idol' (eidolon) and 'Christ' (Christos) against 'Beliar' (Beliar, a name for the adversary), with the rhetorical questions 'what fellowship' (tis koinonia), 'what concord' (tis sumphonesis), 'what agreement' (tis sunkatathesis) denying shared occupancy. Romans 8:9 to 11 uses 'to dwell' (oikeo) and the strengthened compound 'to dwell in' (enoikeo) for the Spirit's settled residence, 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 6:19 use 'inner sanctuary' (naos), the holy heart of a temple, and 1 John 4:4 places 'the one in you' (ho en hymin) above 'the one in the world' (ho en to kosmo) with the perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) 'you have conquered' (nenikekate). The verb 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) occurs 13 times, all in the Gospels, and is never said of a person identified as Spirit-indwelt. Yet the proposition's categorical exclusion, that a believer cannot be possessed, is not stated as a single word. The temple-versus-idol antithesis is rhetorical, not a flat statement of impossibility, and Acts 5:3 uses 'to fill' (pleroo) of Satan filling Ananias' heart inside the believing community, leaving the inhabitation question lexically (at the level of word meaning) underdetermined.

scripture.reasoning: The clause 'greater is the one in you than the one in the world' (meizon estin ho en hymin e ho en to kosmo) says exactly that. The comparative 'greater' (meizon, from megas meaning great) sets the indwelling presence above the worldly adversary, and the location-marker 'in you' (en hymin) marks that presence as inside the addressees. The perfect tense (a completed action whose result still stands) 'you have conquered' (nenikekate) frames the believers as already victorious over the spirits of error. The verse asserts a superior indwelling presence and a settled victory, but it does not contain a verb or clause stating that a demon cannot also inhabit the same person.

The body is called 'a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you' (naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos). The noun 'inner sanctuary' (naos) denotes the holy heart of a temple, the dwelling place of deity, and the relative clause 'whom you have from God' (hou echete apo theou) says the Spirit (pneuma, meaning Spirit or breath) was received from God. The temple image lexically (at the level of word meaning) asserts the Spirit's residence in the believer's body. The exclusion of a rival inhabitant is implied by the temple image but is not stated as a separate proposition, so the force is supportive without being decisive on impossibility.

'Do you not know that you are God's temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?' (ouk oidate hoti naos theou este kai to pneuma tou theou oikei en hymin). The verse pairs 'temple of God' (naos theou) with 'dwells in you' (oikei en hymin), joining the sanctuary noun and the indwelling verb in a single statement and identifying the corporate body of believers as the sanctuary in which God resides. The combination of sanctuary vocabulary and settled-residence verb is the closest the lexicon (the inventory of word meanings) comes to predicating exclusive divine occupancy, though even here the exclusion of a rival inhabitant is left as implication, not as an explicit denial.

'What agreement has the temple of God with idols?' (tis de sunkatathesis nao theou meta eidolon). The rhetorical question lexically (at the level of word meaning) opposes 'temple of God' (naos theou) and 'idol' (eidolon) and answers itself with 'for we are the temple of the living God, as God said, I will dwell among them' (hemeis gar naos theou esmen zontos, kathos eipen ho theos hoti enoikeso en autois). The verb 'I will dwell in' (enoikeo), a strengthened compound of 'to dwell' (oikeo), names God's settled residence, and the immediate antithesis with 'idol' (eidolon) is the strongest lexical expression in the canon of incompatible occupancy. The argument is still rhetorical rather than a categorical impossibility statement, since the noun for a hostile spiritual inhabitant is not the topic of the sentence, but the conceptual incompatibility is asserted directly.

'What concord has Christ with Beliar?' (tis de sumphonesis Christou pros Beliar). 'Beliar' (Beliar) is a New Testament hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) for the adversary, and the noun 'concord' (sumphonesis, literally 'sounding together') is set as impossible between 'Christ' (Christos) and the adversary. The verse adds the lexical incompatibility of Christ and the dark power one verse before the temple-versus-idol antithesis (naos and eidolon), reinforcing the rhetorical denial of shared territory between the two camps. Like the surrounding verses, the impossibility is asserted in the language of fellowship and concord rather than as a flat impossibility of inhabitation.

Paul writes 'if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you' (eiper pneuma theou oikei en hymin). The verb 'to dwell' (oikeo) denotes settled habitation, the same root as a household resident, and the 'if-then' clause-marker 'if indeed' (eiper) treats the indwelling as the assumed mark of belonging to Christ. The closing clause, 'anyone not having the Spirit of Christ is not his', makes Spirit-indwelling the boundary of genuine believing. This anchors the indwelling claim of the proposition.

The compound 'his indwelling Spirit' (enoikoun pneuma) intensifies 'to dwell' (oikeo) with the prefix 'in' (en) and locates the Spirit 'through his Spirit dwelling in you' (dia tou enoikountos autou pneumatos en hymin). The word-form stacks the locative force, so the Spirit is not merely present but resident. The verse reinforces the permanence of the indwelling but speaks only of the Spirit, saying nothing about whether a hostile spirit could share the same body.

'Who has rescued us out of the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son' (hos errusato hemas ek tes exousias tou skotous kai metestesen eis ten basileian tou huiou tes agapes autou). The aorist (a completed past action) 'he rescued' (errusato, from rhuomai meaning to rescue) and 'he transferred' (metestesen, meaning to change residence) describe a completed change of domain. The prepositions 'out of' (ek) and 'into' (eis) frame the believer's location as no longer under 'authority of darkness' (exousia tou skotous). The transfer vocabulary supports the proposition by placing the believer outside the dark sphere, though it speaks to dominion (exousia, meaning ruling authority) rather than to inhabitation as such.

A 'thorn in the flesh' (skolops te sarki) is called 'a messenger of Satan' (angelos Satana), given 'in order that it might buffet me' (hina me kolaphize). The verb 'to buffet' (kolaphizo) means to strike with the fist, to harass, an external assault on a believer, not inhabitation. The lexical content shows a demonic agent afflicting an apostle from without, which directly supports the proposition's clause that believers can be oppressed and harassed while leaving the inhabitation question untouched.

The believer's conflict is 'against the rulers, against the authorities' (pros tas archas, pros tas exousias), 'the spiritual forces of evil' (ta pneumatika tes ponerias). The preposition 'against' (pros) with the accusative case (the noun-form used for the object of an action) frames the relation as combat directed against an external foe, and the repeated 'to stand' (stenai) and 'to stand against' (antistenai) in the surrounding verses cast the believer as one who stands and resists. The vocabulary is military and external. It describes the believer warring against spirits, not hosting them, which fits oppression and harassment rather than possession.

The participle 'the demon-possessed' (daimonizomenous) is applied to the afflicted crowds Jesus heals. Across all 13 occurrences the verb 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) is restricted to the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and is used of the afflicted, the unconverted, or those outside the believing community. It is never said of one identified as indwelt by the Spirit, and the epistolary corpus (the New Testament letters), which has the categories of indwelling and walking-in-the-Spirit, never uses it of anyone. The distribution of the verb is the load-bearing concordance (word-occurrence index) fact, but it is an argument from how the word is used rather than from any verse stating the exclusion, so it constrains the case without closing it.

Peter asks 'why has Satan filled your heart' (dia ti eplerosen ho Satanas ten kardian sou) to lie to the Holy Spirit. The aorist (a completed past action) 'he filled' (eplerosen, from pleroo meaning to fill), applied to a man within the believing community and paired with 'Satan' (Satanas) as agent, is the principal complicating datum. One reading takes 'to fill' (pleroo) the heart as a strong satanic influence short of bodily inhabitation, since 'to fill' (pleroo) elsewhere takes abstract objects like joy, knowledge, fruit of righteousness. Another reading takes it as evidence that one counted among the believers could be deeply controlled. The word 'to fill' (pleroo) does not by itself decide between influence and inhabitation, which keeps the proposition contested.

'A daughter of Abraham, whom Satan had bound for 18 years' (thugatera Abraam ousan, hen edesen ho Satanas idou deka kai okto ete). The participle 'being' (ousan) presents her present status as a daughter of Abraham (a phrase Luke uses positively for a member of the covenant community), and 'he bound' (edesen, aorist of deo meaning to bind, a completed past action) describes a sustained satanic binding that produced a physical infirmity. The verse is sometimes invoked against the proposition because a covenant insider is shown under sustained satanic constraint, but the vocabulary describes binding and infirmity, not 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) inhabitation. It illustrates oppression of a covenant participant rather than possession of a Spirit-indwelt New Covenant believer.

complicating_texts.resolution: The statement that Satan filled (the verb 'to fill', pleroo) the heart of Ananias is the strongest text against a clean separation of believer from demonic inhabitation. It is addressed by observing that 'to fill' (pleroo) of the heart describes the saturating influence of a motive or agent rather than the bodily inhabitation denoted by 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai), and that the narrative never calls Ananias demon-possessed. The tension is acknowledged, not eliminated, because the verb itself does not settle whether the filling was inhabitation or intense influence, and the bundle supplies no grammatical layer to adjudicate.

The bound daughter of Abraham is addressed by observing that 'to bind' (deo) and the infirmity vocabulary describe sustained external constraint rather than inhabitation. The Lukan text describes a member of the covenant community under Satan's grip but does not use 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai), 'having a demon' (daimonion echon), or any inhabitation word. The verse therefore complicates a strong reading of the proposition by widening what Satan can do to a covenant member but does not lexically (at the level of word meaning) equate that to possession in the technical sense the proposition denies.

The temple image ('inner sanctuary', naos) implies an exclusive divine occupancy, since a sanctuary is set apart for one resident deity, and so it weighs toward the proposition. It is addressed but not made decisive because the inference from the image to the impossibility of a second inhabitant is a synthetic step. The image strongly suggests exclusivity but does not state it as a denial, so the image supports without proving the exclusion.

The proposition leans heavily on the fact that 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) is never applied to a believer. This distributional silence is a real and consistent pattern across all 13 occurrences (all in the Gospels, never in the epistles, that is the New Testament letters), which is why the indwelling half of the claim is well supported, but an argument from the absence of a predication cannot by itself yield a categorical impossibility. The pattern constrains the verdict toward the proposition while leaving the universal exclusion lexically (at the level of word meaning) unproven.

variants.note: All cited verses lie outside the open-cbgm 3 John sample, so CBGM data (the manuscript-relationship method used in the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) was not consulted and ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) status is treated as shadow. The bundle reports an empty variant_units list and not_in_ecm_scope true. The bracketed surface readings visible in Romans 8:11, 2 Corinthians 12:7, and Ephesians 6:10 to 18 are minor word-order and spelling variants that do not touch 'to dwell' (oikeo), 'to dwell in' (enoikeo), 'inner sanctuary' (naos), 'idol' (eidolon), 'Beliar' (Beliar), 'the one in you' (ho en hymin), 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai), 'to fill' (pleroo), or 'to buffet' (kolaphizo), so the disputed verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the sanctuary noun 'inner sanctuary' (naos) plus the verbs 'to dwell' (oikeo) and 'to dwell in' (enoikeo) in 1 Corinthians 3:16, 1 Corinthians 6:19, Romans 8:9 to 11, and 2 Corinthians 6:16, the comparative 'greater' (meizon) of 1 John 4:4, and the explicit antithesis of 'temple of God' (naos theou) with 'idol' (eidolon) and Christ with 'Beliar' (Beliar) in 2 Corinthians 6:14 to 16 as together establishing that the Spirit's exclusive occupancy of the believer's body rules out simultaneous demonic inhabitation. The transfer vocabulary of Colossians 1:13 ('to rescue', rhuomai, out of the 'authority' (exousia) of darkness) is read as a completed change of domain, and the consistent restriction of 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) to the Gospels and to the unconverted is read as confirmation. Acts 5:3 is read as 'to fill' (pleroo) of influence, not bodily inhabitation. On this lens the proposition is affirmed.

Reads Acts 5:3 (Satan filling the heart of one within the community), Luke 13:16 (a daughter of Abraham bound by Satan for 18 years), and the harassment language of 2 Corinthians 12:7 as evidence that a covenant member or even genuine believer can be subject to a demon in or affecting the body. Notes that the indwelling texts establish the Spirit's presence without containing a flat denial of demonic co-habitation, that the 2 Corinthians 6:14 to 16 antithesis is rhetorical question (incompatibility of fellowship) not a categorical metaphysical impossibility, and that the 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) distribution is silence, not predication. On this lens the proposition overreaches the explicit lexical (word-meaning) data.

Treats Colossians 1:13 'he rescued out of the authority of darkness' (errusato ek tes exousias tou skotous) and the location-shift from 'in the flesh' (en sarki) to 'in the Spirit' (en pneumati) in Romans 8:9 as a transfer of dominion rather than a guarantee about every kind of demonic engagement. On this lens the believer is removed from the dark sphere's authority and so the proposition holds at the level of dominion and lordship, while leaving room for harassment, oppression, and severe attack short of full 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) possession.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on whether the indwelling and temple vocabulary plus the 2 Corinthians 6 antithesis entail an exclusion of demonic inhabitation, and on whether 'to fill' (pleroo) in Acts 5:3 and 'to bind' (deo) in Luke 13:16 denote inhabitation or sustained external control. The principle of letting Scripture interpret Scripture (analogia scripturae) links the indwelling texts ('to dwell' oikeo, 'to dwell in' enoikeo, 'inner sanctuary' naos) to the 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) distribution but yields a strongly supported indwelling claim alongside an inference-dependent exclusion.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: The relationship between the Spirit's indwelling of a believer and the possibility of a demon inhabiting that same person; whether the canon treats demonic possession ('to be demon-possessed', daimonizomai) and Spirit-indwelling as mutually exclusive states, and how the categories possession, inhabitation, oppression, and harassment map onto the lexicon (the inventory of word meanings).
stem_audit.notes: The proposition embeds its conclusion by asserting that a genuine believer cannot be possessed, which states the disputed exclusion as a settled premise. It also preloads the contrast between possession and the categories oppressed, tempted, and harassed, importing a taxonomy (classification scheme) that the texts support in part but do not name as a fixed three-tier scheme. The verdict was derived on the original stem, and the neutralized form is recorded only to expose the preloading.

lay_summary: The Greek behind these verses cleanly establishes the first part of the claim, that the Holy Spirit truly lives inside a believer. Romans 8 uses the verb 'to dwell' (oikeo) and its stronger compound 'to dwell in' (enoikeo), both meaning to dwell as a settled resident. First Corinthians 3 and 6 call the body and the gathered believers a 'naos', the inner sanctuary of a temple, the place set apart for God. Second Corinthians 6 sharpens this by asking what agreement the temple of God has with idols ('eidolon') and what concord Christ has with 'Beliar' (a name for the adversary), naming the Spirit's residence (enoikeo) and immediately denying any fellowship between the holy dwelling and a hostile spiritual rival. First John 4 says the one who is in you is greater than the one in the world. Colossians 1 says God has rescued the believer out of the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his Son, language of a completed change of domain. So the texts plainly assert a real, settled, superior presence of the Spirit in the believer and a deliberate antithesis between the believer's inner sanctuary and any rival inhabitant. The second part of the claim, that this presence makes it impossible for a demon to inhabit the same person, is where the words stop short. No verse contains a flat statement denying that a demon can inhabit a believer. The strongest support is a pattern rather than a sentence: the verb 'to be demon-possessed' (daimonizomai) occurs 13 times and is restricted to the Gospels, never used of anyone identified as Spirit-indwelt, and never used in the epistles at all. That consistent silence points toward the claim but cannot by itself prove a flat impossibility. The verses about Paul show a messenger of Satan buffeting him, the verb 'to buffet' (kolaphizo) meaning to strike from outside, which fits the idea that believers are harassed and oppressed rather than inhabited. The hardest verses the other way are Acts 5, where Satan is said to fill the heart of Ananias inside the believing community, and Luke 13, where a daughter of Abraham is bound by Satan for 18 years. The verbs there, 'to fill' (pleroo) and 'to bind' (deo), can mean either deep influence and external constraint, or something more, and they do not settle the question. Because the indwelling half is well grounded and reinforced by the 2 Corinthians 6 antithesis, while the categorical exclusion still depends on inference from how words are used rather than on a direct statement, the lexical (word-meaning) finding is disputed rather than fully confirmed.
